title: Shopping List
story: Mom hands you the grocery list: milk, eggs, bread, apples, and cheese. She asks you to read each item out loud. Instead of reading them yourself, you write a program that goes through the list automatically, printing each item one by one!
why: Lists are everywhere in programming � todo items, friend names, game inventory, song playlists. `for` loops let you visit each item in a list without writing repetitive code.
analogy: A for loop is like reading names off a class roster � you point to each name, say it out loud, and move to the next one until the list is done.
try_it: Add 'chocolate' to the shopping list and run the program again. Then create a list of your favorite snacks and print them all with 'I love ' before each one. Can you make a list of numbers and print each one multiplied by 2 inside the loop?
tips: The loop variable (like `item`) is created automatically � no `let` or `var` needed.
Use descriptive names: `for friend in friends`, `for snack in snacks`.
Lists use square brackets with commas between items: `["a", "b", "c"]`.
You can do anything inside a for loop � print, do math, build strings, even use `if`/`else`.
common_mistakes: Writing `for item = in list` instead of `for item in list` � no equals sign, just `in`.
Using `let` before the loop variable: `for let item in list` � the loop creates the variable automatically.
Forgetting commas between list items: `["milk" "eggs" "bread"]` won't work � each item must be separated by a comma.
Trying to use a `for` loop with just a number range like `for i in 1..10` � use a `while` loop for counting.
